![](images/ds-venn-2010-vs-2026.png){fig-alt="Two data science Venn diagrams, one above the other: Drew Conway's 2010 version with hacking skills, maths and statistics and substantive expertise, and below it a 2026 version measured from job ads with software engineering and deployment, statistics and inference, and LLM and agent engineering"}

## What this is

Every job ad a personal crawler collected for data and AI roles hiring in Germany, EU-wide remote, worldwide remote or the UK — **{{< var jobskills.n_ads >}} de-duplicated ads, {{< var jobskills.months >}}**. Each was read in full by a model judge and scored against a fixed vocabulary of {{< var jobskills.n_skills >}} skills in {{< var jobskills.n_areas >}} areas, one question per skill, so the same question is answered for every ad and the numbers compare across titles.

Six findings:

1. Under Drew Conway's 2010 circles, {{< var jobskills.conway_all_three >}}% of ads land in the centre, {{< var jobskills.conway_danger_zone >}}% in the "danger zone" he thought nearly empty, and {{< var jobskills.conway_outside_pct >}}% require at least one skill none of his circles covers.
2. "Data Scientist" and "AI Engineer" are {{< var jobskills.d_ai_engineer__data_scientist >}} apart on their requirement profiles — further than Data Scientist is from Data Analyst ({{< var jobskills.d_data_analyst__data_scientist >}}). Statistics divides them: {{< var jobskills.data_scientist_statistics >}}% against {{< var jobskills.ai_engineer_statistics >}}%.
3. The titles form three branches, not two. "ML Engineer" is the only short step between the engineering and inference branches ({{< var jobskills.d_data_scientist__ml_engineer >}} from Data Scientist, {{< var jobskills.d_ai_engineer__ml_engineer >}} from AI Engineer).
4. Data Engineer and Analytics Engineer are the closest pair on the map ({{< var jobskills.closest_pair_d >}}). Data governance marks that branch: {{< var jobskills.analytics_engineer_data_governance >}}% and {{< var jobskills.data_engineer_data_governance >}}% of their ads, against {{< var jobskills.data_governance_elsewhere >}}% elsewhere.
5. Data Scientist, AI Engineer and ML Engineer ads share exactly {{< var jobskills.n_core_shared >}} skills: {{< var jobskills.core_shared >}}. Beyond those five, Data Scientist and AI Engineer have nothing in common.
6. The most-required skill is not technical: stakeholder communication, {{< var jobskills.all_stakeholder_comms >}}% of ads, ahead of Python at {{< var jobskills.all_python >}}%. {{< var jobskills.ai_no_python >}}% of "AI Engineer" ads do not require Python at all.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Population and sample {.unnumbered}

- **{{< var jobskills.n_ads >}} job ads**, de-duplicated, with a data / AI title: AI Engineer {{< var jobskills.n_ai_engineer >}}, Data Scientist {{< var jobskills.n_data_scientist >}}, Data Engineer {{< var jobskills.n_data_engineer >}}, Forward Deployed {{< var jobskills.n_forward_deployed >}}, Data Analyst {{< var jobskills.n_data_analyst >}}, ML Engineer {{< var jobskills.n_ml_engineer >}}, Research Scientist {{< var jobskills.n_research_scientist >}}, Analytics Engineer {{< var jobskills.n_analytics_engineer >}}, Quantitative Researcher {{< var jobskills.n_quantitative_researcher >}}.
- **Where they hire:** Germany, EU-wide remote, worldwide remote, or the UK. Live {{< var jobskills.months >}}.
- **Where they come from:** employers' own boards and careers pages, aggregators, and a curated feed — the published data carries no source or employer, and the same opening reached by two routes counts once (matched on URL and on company + title).
- **Not a random sample of the market.** It is the ads a personal crawler targets, so it describes what these titles ask for, not how many of each exist.
:::

## Which titles are hiring

![](images/roles.png){fig-alt="Bar chart of the nine job-title families as a share of the ads"}

"AI Engineer" is the most frequent title at {{< var jobskills.pct_ai_engineer >}}%, then Data Scientist ({{< var jobskills.pct_data_scientist >}}%) and Data Engineer ({{< var jobskills.pct_data_engineer >}}%); Analytics Engineer ({{< var jobskills.pct_analytics_engineer >}}%) and Quantitative Researcher ({{< var jobskills.pct_quantitative_researcher >}}%) are the rarest. Titles come from the ad itself, by regular expression over the job title; "AI Engineer" includes variants such as "Senior Software Engineer – AI".

## Conway's circles, measured

In September 2010 Drew Conway drew three overlapping circles — hacking skills, maths and statistics, substantive expertise — with data science in the middle and **"danger zone!"** where code met domain knowledge without statistics. His were freehand and carried no numbers. Here they are sized by how many of the {{< var jobskills.n_ads >}} ads land in each; an ad joins a circle if it requires at least one skill mapped to it.

![](images/conway-measured.png){fig-alt="Conway's three circles redrawn with region areas proportional to the share of job ads in each"}

{{< var jobskills.conway_danger_zone >}}% of ads ask for code and domain engagement but require no statistics — the second-largest region, behind the centre ({{< var jobskills.conway_all_three >}}%) and larger than his "machine learning" ({{< var jobskills.conway_ml_only >}}%) and "traditional research" ({{< var jobskills.conway_trad_research >}}%) lenses combined.

{{< var jobskills.conway_outside_n >}} of the tracked skills — LLM applications, agents, RAG, evaluation, fine-tuning, observability, responsible AI — fit none of the three circles. **{{< var jobskills.conway_outside_pct >}}% of ads require at least one**, rising to {{< var jobskills.genai_ai_engineer >}}% of AI Engineer ads, and the share is flat across every month in the sample.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Sources and permissions {.unnumbered}

Conway's diagram is reproduced with attribution from [drewconway.com](http://drewconway.com/zia/2013/3/26/the-data-science-venn-diagram) (Drew Conway, *The Data Science Venn Diagram*, 2010). Only the measured figures and the 2026 circles are this page's own.
:::

## The 2026 circles

![](images/ds-venn-2026.png){fig-alt="A 2026 data science Venn diagram with three equal circles — software engineering and deployment, statistics and inference, LLM and agent engineering — with the overlaps named data science, analytics and forecasting, AI engineering and applied research"}

The same diagram with circles chosen to fit what the ads cluster into. Two are Conway's under new names; one is new.

- **Software engineering & deployment** — his hacking skills, {{< var jobskills.v26_swe >}}% of ads, the largest circle. Model serving alone is required in {{< var jobskills.all_model_serving_pct >}}%. Building and shipping are not separate trades: {{< var jobskills.pct_build_and_deploy >}}% of ads require both, {{< var jobskills.pct_build_only >}}% building without deployment, {{< var jobskills.pct_deploy_only >}}% deployment without building.
- **Statistics & inference** — his maths and statistics, {{< var jobskills.v26_inference >}}% of ads, the one circle that survives intact. Deep learning and NLP have left it for the LLM circle; product analytics and BI have joined it.
- **LLM & agent engineering** — new, {{< var jobskills.v26_llm >}}% of ads.
- **Substantive expertise stops being a circle.** Stakeholder communication appears in {{< var jobskills.all_stakeholder_comms >}}% of ads, too universal to divide anyone.

By region: data science (all three circles) is {{< var jobskills.v26_datascience >}}% of ads, against {{< var jobskills.conway_all_three >}}% under Conway's. **AI engineering** — engineering and LLM work with no inference requirement, Conway's danger zone — is the largest lens at {{< var jobskills.v26_aieng >}}%, with {{< var jobskills.v26_aieng_titled >}}% of its ads titled AI Engineer. **Analytics & forecasting** is {{< var jobskills.v26_analytics >}}%, **applied research** {{< var jobskills.v26_research >}}%.

## Building a model versus calling one

{{< var jobskills.bc_train >}}% of ads require building or training a model (classical ML, deep learning, fine-tuning, computer vision, recommenders); {{< var jobskills.bc_call >}}% require calling one (LLM applications, retrieval, agents, observability). Only {{< var jobskills.bc_both >}}% require both. {{< var jobskills.bc_call_only >}}% want the API work with no model-building at all, against {{< var jobskills.bc_train_only >}}% that build without ever touching an API. Fine-tuning, the skill between them, is required in {{< var jobskills.bc_finetune >}}%.

![](images/build-vs-call.png){fig-alt="Chart comparing the share of each job title's ads that require building or training a model against the share that require calling one over an API"}

By title: ML Engineer {{< var jobskills.bc_ml_engineer_train >}}% build, Research Scientist {{< var jobskills.bc_research_scientist_train >}}%, Data Scientist {{< var jobskills.bc_data_scientist_train >}}%. AI Engineer inverts it — {{< var jobskills.bc_ai_engineer_call >}}% call an API, {{< var jobskills.bc_ai_engineer_train >}}% build. Analytics Engineer is the clean case: {{< var jobskills.bc_analytics_engineer_train >}}% build, {{< var jobskills.bc_analytics_engineer_call >}}% call.

Machine learning of any kind is required in {{< var jobskills.ml_any_pct >}}% of ads (classical {{< var jobskills.ml_classical_pct >}}%, deep learning {{< var jobskills.ml_deep_pct >}}%); the LLM stack in {{< var jobskills.ml_llmstack_pct >}}%. {{< var jobskills.ml_llm_no_ml_pct >}}% of ads want the LLM stack and require no machine learning, against {{< var jobskills.ml_ml_no_llm_pct >}}% the reverse.

Machine learning is not a circle on the 2026 diagram because it does not divide the market. Drawn generously it covers {{< var jobskills.mlc_pct >}}% of ads ({{< var jobskills.mlc_n >}}), of which {{< var jobskills.mlc_inside_any_pct >}}% already fall inside one of the three circles and {{< var jobskills.mlc_in_centre_pct >}}% in the dead centre; a circle of its own would enclose {{< var jobskills.mlc_alone_n >}} ads. It runs through the three — {{< var jobskills.mlc_covers_swe >}}% of the engineering circle, {{< var jobskills.mlc_covers_inf >}}% of inference, {{< var jobskills.mlc_covers_llm >}}% of the LLM circle. Where it is required it has moved toward engineering: {{< var jobskills.ml_serving_pct >}}% of ML ads require model serving, against {{< var jobskills.ml_serving_rest_pct >}}% of the rest.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Is machine learning simply assumed in a data science ad? {.unnumbered}

Partly. Of the {{< var jobskills.mlx_ds_ads >}} Data Scientist ads, {{< var jobskills.mlx_silent_ads >}} never use the words machine learning, deep learning or neural network — but {{< var jobskills.mlx_silent_naming_tool_pct >}}% of those do name a technique or tool that is unmistakably machine learning. Correcting for that raises the figure from {{< var jobskills.mlx_haiku_named >}}% to about {{< var jobskills.mlx_implied_total_pct >}}%, which lands on the independent estimate from the other direction ({{< var jobskills.mlx_jev_any_level >}}% detected at some level).

The remaining {{< var jobskills.mlx_silent_nothing >}} ads ({{< var jobskills.mlx_silent_nothing_pct >}}% of Data Scientist ads) name neither the concept nor any of its tools. They ask for Python, SQL, A/B testing, causal inference, R, dbt, Tableau and stakeholder communication instead.
:::

## Three branches, not a rebrand

Scored on what each ad requires, the {{< var jobskills.n_titles >}} titles arrange into three branches:

- **Engineering** — AI Engineer, ML Engineer, Forward Deployed, Research Scientist. LLM applications, agents, NLP, model serving, evals, CI/CD. Statistics is required in {{< var jobskills.ai_engineer_statistics >}}% of AI Engineer ads.
- **Inference** — Quantitative Researcher, Data Scientist, Data Analyst. Statistics, experimentation, forecasting, SQL, BI. Quant ads are the extreme: {{< var jobskills.quantitative_researcher_statistics >}}% statistics, {{< var jobskills.quantitative_researcher_forecasting >}}% forecasting.
- **Data** — Data Engineer and Analytics Engineer. Pipelines ({{< var jobskills.data_engineer_pipelines_etl >}}% and {{< var jobskills.analytics_engineer_pipelines_etl >}}%), warehouse, dbt, cloud, and almost no statistics ({{< var jobskills.data_engineer_statistics >}}% and {{< var jobskills.analytics_engineer_statistics >}}%). Analytics Engineer is not a flavour of Data Analyst ({{< var jobskills.d_analytics_engineer__data_analyst >}} away) but the analyst-facing end of data engineering — SQL in {{< var jobskills.analytics_engineer_sql >}}% of its ads, dbt in {{< var jobskills.analytics_engineer_dbt_modelling >}}%.

The tail is the specialist end: {{< var jobskills.tail_skills >}}.

## Where the number comes from {.unnumbered}

These are not every skill an ad might mention — they are a *fixed vocabulary* the judge is asked about, one question per skill, so the same question is answered for every ad and the percentages compare across titles. A free-for-all count of whatever words appear cannot do that, because no two employers use the same words.

The list is curated but not frozen: {{< var jobskills.n_skills >}} skills across {{< var jobskills.n_areas >}} areas, and it grows when the evidence says it should. [How that works](#method) is at the foot of the page.
:::

## The titles, by distance between what they require

Each title's profile is the share of its ads requiring each of the {{< var jobskills.n_skills >}} skills; an edge is the Euclidean distance between two profiles, so smaller means more alike. Beside it, the skills that most separate the pair.

{{< include _titles-diagram.qmd >}}

Blue is the inference branch, orange engineering, purple data; "ML Engineer" is the hinge. Solid edges trace the chain from one end of the market to the other, dashed edges the nearest neighbour of a side title.

The market is a chain, not a cluster: Quantitative Researcher → Data Scientist → ML Engineer → AI Engineer, every step between {{< var jobskills.d_ai_engineer__ml_engineer >}} and {{< var jobskills.d_data_scientist__quantitative_researcher >}}, while the direct Data Scientist to AI Engineer distance is {{< var jobskills.d_ai_engineer__data_scientist >}}. Data Engineer and Analytics Engineer sit at **{{< var jobskills.closest_pair_d >}}, the shortest distance on the map**, and that branch touches the rest only through Data Analyst.

## Shared core, separate specialisms

![](images/core-skills-venn.png){fig-alt="Venn diagram of the core skills of Data Scientist, AI Engineer and ML Engineer ads"}

![](images/skills-ds-vs-ai-scatter.png){fig-alt="Scatter plot of every tracked skill: share of Data Scientist ads requiring each skill against share of AI Engineer ads"}

The three titles share a {{< var jobskills.n_core_shared >}}-skill core, and it is a professional one rather than a specialism: {{< var jobskills.core_shared >}}. Beyond those five, Data Scientist and AI Engineer ads have nothing in common. Statistics, SQL, classical ML, A/B experimentation, forecasting and product analytics belong to Data Scientist alone; LLM applications, agents, NLP, RAG, APIs and responsible AI to AI Engineer alone. ML Engineer shares the same five and adds MLOps tooling, containers and deep learning. Software engineering is the biggest shared one: {{< var jobskills.ai_engineer_software_engineering >}}% of AI Engineer ads and {{< var jobskills.data_scientist_software_engineering >}}% of Data Scientist ads.

Each Venn region is "required by these titles and *not* the others", so the Data Scientist / AI Engineer lens is empty: everything those two share, ML Engineer requires as well. A core skill is one required in at least {{< var jobskills.core_pct >}}% of a title's ads; the circles are drawn equal, so only the lists carry information. The scatter is the same data without the threshold.

## Method

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## How the skills were scored {.unnumbered}

Scores come from the production pipeline of **jobcrawler**, a personal job-board crawler that scrapes employer ATS boards, filters by title and location with deterministic rules, and stores each ad. After storage every ad is read once by **Jev** (TypeSafe's System One model, version {{< var jobskills.judge_version >}}), which answers typed questions over the ad and returns probabilities rather than text.

- For each of **{{< var jobskills.n_skills >}} tracked skills** Jev is asked one four-level question: does the ad *not involve* the skill, *mention it in passing*, list it as *nice to have*, or *require* it. One question per skill, so an answer cannot contradict itself.
- An ad counts as requiring the skill when "required" reaches a probability of 0.6. Most skill-by-ad judgements come back "not involved", and roughly one in six reaches "required".
- Jev has no part in choosing the ads: the pool is gathered and filtered by rules, and the title families come from regular expressions over the title.
- Cost: about 6k input tokens per ad, under a cent.

The scores are model judgements, consistent across titles but never checked against human labels: treat the percentages as what a careful reader of the ad would conclude, with a few points of noise. **"Required" is a high bar** — every percentage here counts ads where the skill reaches *required*, not ads that mention it. Across all judged ads, {{< var jobskills.mlcheck_all_jev_mentioned >}}% mention machine learning by Jev's reading and {{< var jobskills.mlcheck_all_haiku_named >}}% by the second model's, against {{< var jobskills.mlcheck_all_jev_required >}}% that reach *required*. Agreement on the required call is moderate (Cohen's κ ≈ {{< var jobskills.mlcheck_kappa >}}), so treat an individual figure as approximate and the direction as solid.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## How the skill list grows, and who decides {.unnumbered}

There are **two passes over every ad**.

**Pass one — Jev, the scorer.** The fixed vocabulary above. Same questions, every ad, probabilities out. Every percentage on this page is built from it, and it is the only reason the percentages compare across titles.

**Pass two — an open-vocabulary extraction.** Every ad is also read by a small, cheap model (Claude Haiku), five ads to a call, with one instruction: list every skill, tool or method this ad asks for, **in the ad's own words**, say whether it is required or nice to have, and quote the sentence that shows it. Nothing is matched against the vocabulary at this stage — the model does not know the vocabulary exists.

That covers the whole pool: **{{< var jobskills.mentions_total >}} skill mentions** across **{{< var jobskills.mentions_phrases >}} distinct phrases**, of which {{< var jobskills.mentions_phrases_in_10_ads_or_more >}} appear in ten ads or more. A deterministic alias table maps each phrase onto a vocabulary skill where the mapping is obvious — "PostgreSQL" to SQL, "Kubernetes" to containers, "RLHF" to deep learning. {{< var jobskills.mentions_pct_mapped >}}% of all mentions map. **The rest are the point**: the things ads keep asking for that the vocabulary has no question for, ranked by how many jobs require them.

A weekly review reads that ranking and proposes additions, which a human accepts or rejects — the vocabulary is never edited automatically, because adding a skill re-scores every ad. The review of {{< var jobskills.mentions_review_date >}} accepted four: **software engineering** (named in {{< var jobskills.mentions_accepted_software_engineering >}} jobs), **data governance** ({{< var jobskills.mentions_accepted_data_governance >}}), **APIs and integration** ({{< var jobskills.mentions_accepted_apis_services >}}) and **responsible AI** ({{< var jobskills.mentions_accepted_responsible_ai >}}). Three frequent phrases were rejected: "problem-solving" ({{< var jobskills.mentions_rejected_problem_solving >}} jobs) and English and German ({{< var jobskills.mentions_rejected_languages >}} between them) are traits and languages rather than skills, and "data science" ({{< var jobskills.mentions_rejected_data_science >}}) is the name of the field.

Adding "software engineering" overturned one of this page's own findings — before it was tracked, Data Scientist and AI Engineer appeared to share no core skill at all. That is what the second pass is for. Every figure regenerates from the same scripts whenever the vocabulary moves (vocabulary as of {{< var jobskills.vocab_date >}}).
:::

## Data

The underlying data is published alongside this page: [**download it here**](data/ai-data-job-skills.csv), with a [**companion list of the skills**](data/skills.json) and their areas.

It holds one row per job ad — the title, which title family it falls into, the hiring region, the month, its position on the map, and a yes/no flag for each of the {{< var jobskills.n_skills >}} skills. Deliberately not included: employer names, links, or any of the ad text. That is enough to redraw every chart here and check any number in it, without republishing anyone's job postings.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## How the charts were drawn {.unnumbered}

Charts are drawn with [plotnine](https://plotnine.org) for the static figures and [Plotly](https://plotly.com/python/), styled to match, for the interactive map. Colours come from the Okabe-Ito colour-blind-safe palette, and wherever more than three categories share a plot, marker shape carries the identity as well as the colour.
:::
